deep.reconstruction:
The page contains four research or bibliographic notes and no derivations. Context: the next page is Hilbert's 'Plan für meine künftigen zahlentheoretischen Studien' (relative-abelian fields, class fields, quinary forms), which places this page around 1897-1900.

(1) Bibliographic note pasted in on a slip: Paolo Bonaventura, 'Sul teorema di reciprocità della teoria dei residui quadratici pei numeri interi del campo (1, i√2)', Giornale di Matematiche vol. XXX (1892). In modern terms this is quadratic reciprocity in the ring of integers of Q(i, √2) = Q(ζ_8). Hilbert was collecting literature on reciprocity laws in algebraic number fields, presumably for the Zahlbericht and his relative-quadratic theory.

(2) 'Wasserhose' (waterspout): the one-sheeted hyperboloid as an equilibrium figure, after Dirichlet, with pressure relations. This refers to the Dirichlet (1860) / Dedekind / Riemann theory of rotating homogeneous fluid masses with linear velocity fields, where quadric surfaces appear as free surfaces. It is a reading or lecture note, not developed.

(3) Methodological remark: the proof that the class field exists, and also the proof of the reciprocity laws, is easier in the special case where the class field is assumed Galois (presumably over Q, or over a ground field larger than the base field k). This is a programmatic statement. Behind it is the observation that when K/Q is Galois one can exploit the action of Gal(K/Q) on ideal classes and on norm residues. This is the setting Hilbert actually used in his relative-quadratic work (1899-1902), where he constructed class fields only in special cases (e.g. class number 2).

(4) Two proposed routes to the most general biquadratic reciprocity law (in Q(i), including the supplementary laws):
(a) Reduce it to the quadratic law by means of quadratic class fields. That is, apply the quadratic reciprocity law (Hilbert's norm-residue symbol / product formula) in suitable fields such as Q(i), Q(ζ_8) and relative quadratic extensions of them.
(b) Directly compute the value of α^{(N(𝔭)-1)/4} mod 𝔭. This is Euler's criterion defining the quartic residue symbol: (α/𝔭)_4 ≡ α^{(N𝔭-1)/4} (mod 𝔭), which is a fourth root of unity.

No computations are carried out on the page.

checkable.sympy: from sympy import I, expand, simplify; simplify(expand((8 + I)*(3 - 2*I))/13) == 2 - I
checkable.asserts: 8 + i is divisible by 3 + 2i, i.e. 2^((13-1)/4) = 8 ≡ -i = i^3 mod (3+2i). So the quartic residue symbol (2/(3+2i))_4 = -i, illustrating the Euler criterion α^{(N𝔭-1)/4}.
2 is a quartic residue mod 73 = 3^2 + 64*1^2 (Gauss: 2 is a quartic residue mod p iff p = x^2 + 64 y^2).
2 is not a quartic residue mod 13, consistent with 13 not being of the form x^2 + 64 y^2.
